concepts.name: Royal Charter of 1600: Legal Basis and Monopoly Grant
key_dimensions: Exact date (31 December 1600) and the reigning monarch (Queen Elizabeth I) — common trap on 'who granted' vs 'who petitioned'
Nature of monopoly: exclusive trading rights east of the Cape of Good Hope for 15 years, renewable — scope and geographic limits
Legal personality: Company as a 'body corporate and politic' — earliest example of joint-stock corporate structure in Indian context
Distinction between the Charter's trading monopoly and later political/territorial powers (which came from subsequent charters)

concepts.name: Merchant Consortium Behind the Company: Founders and Initial Capital
key_dimensions: The group of 218 London merchants and mercers who petitioned Elizabeth I — not a state enterprise, purely private origin
Initial subscribed capital of £72,000 — significance of joint-stock model vs. regulated company model
Role of Thomas Smythe (first Governor) — distinction between the 'Governor' of the Company and later political governors
Comparison with Portuguese Estado da India (state-sponsored) and Dutch VOC (semi-state) — UPSC loves comparative questions

concepts.name: Governance Structure of the Early Company: Court of Proprietors and Court of Directors
key_dimensions: Court of Proprietors (General Court) — shareholders with voting rights based on stock held; democratic but plutocratic
Court of Directors (24 directors) — day-to-day management; elected annually by Proprietors
Governor and Deputy Governor roles within the Court of Directors — not to be confused with colonial governors
How this internal structure became the template for later Parliamentary oversight debates (Regulating Act 1773 context)

concepts.name: Early Voyages (1601–1612): From Red Sea to Surat
key_dimensions: First voyage (1601) under James Lancaster — Cape of Good Hope route to Aceh and Bantam (Southeast Asia, NOT India directly)
Distinction: early EIC focused on Southeast Asia (spices) before pivoting to Indian subcontinent — a common misconception trap
Sixth voyage and the Battle of Swally (1612) under Thomas Best — first naval victory over Portuguese, opening door to Mughal favour
Sequential shift: spice trade → cloth-spice exchange → Indian textiles — evolving commercial logic

concepts.name: Battle of Swally (1612): Strategic and Diplomatic Turning Point
key_dimensions: Commander Thomas Best defeated Portuguese fleet near Surat — significance for English naval credibility in Indian Ocean
Immediate diplomatic consequence: Mughal Emperor Jahangir's permission to trade at Surat (1613 farman)
Why Mughals favoured English over Portuguese: Portuguese interference with Hajj pilgrim ships — a nuanced UPSC angle
Distinction: Swally granted trading access, NOT a factory; first factory at Surat came separately in 1613

concepts.name: First English Factory at Surat (1608–1613): Process and Significance
key_dimensions: William Hawkins's mission (1608–1611): first English emissary to Jahangir's court — personal favour from Jahangir but no firm trading rights secured
Thomas Roe's embassy (1615–1619) under James I — secured a formal imperial farman; distinction between Hawkins (informal) and Roe (formal diplomatic mission)
1613 factory at Surat: first permanent English trading post in India — 'factory' meaning (a trading post with a 'factor'/agent, NOT a manufacturing unit)
Surat as the headquarters of EIC in India until superseded by Bombay (1687) — chronological trap

concepts.name: Thomas Roe's Embassy (1615–1619): Diplomacy and Its Limits
key_dimensions: Roe sent by King James I — represents a state-level diplomatic recognition of the Company's importance
Secured a farman from Jahangir allowing trade and a factory at Surat — but no territorial concessions
Roe's famous advice: EIC should avoid territorial expansion and focus on trade ('the sea trade will be the best and surest')  — irony given later history, a favourite UPSC quote
Comparison with later Mughal-EIC interactions under Aurangzeb — deterioration of the relationship Roe built

concepts.name: Competing European Companies: EIC vs. VOC (Dutch East India Company)
key_dimensions: VOC founded in 1602 — two years after EIC; larger capital (10× EIC's initial capital), semi-state backing
Anglo-Dutch rivalry: Amboyna Massacre (1623) — Dutch killed English merchants in Indonesia, effectively pushing EIC from Southeast Asia toward India
Consequence of Amboyna: EIC's strategic retreat to India becomes permanent — a causal link UPSC tests
Structural differences: VOC had permanent joint-stock from outset; EIC initially had voyage-by-voyage investment until 1657 permanent stock

concepts.name: Amboyna Massacre (1623) and Its Impact on EIC's India Strategy
key_dimensions: Dutch execution of English merchants at Ambon in the Moluccas — alleged conspiracy charge
Forced EIC to effectively abandon the Spice Islands (Moluccas) to the Dutch
Redirected EIC focus firmly to Indian subcontinent trade (textiles, indigo, saltpeter) — pivot with long-term consequences
Diplomatic fallout: strained Anglo-Dutch relations, but no immediate war — EIC had to absorb the loss; UPSC trap: this did NOT immediately cause a war

concepts.name: EIC Charter Renewals and Monopoly Challenges (1609–1657)
key_dimensions: 1609 renewal by James I — made the monopoly perpetual (no fixed term) unless revoked with 3 years' notice
Interlopers and 'free traders': merchants outside the Company challenging monopoly — parliamentary debates on free trade vs. monopoly
Courteen's Association (1635): rival company licensed by Charles I — shows monopoly was politically contested even early on
1657 Cromwell's Charter: reorganised Company under Commonwealth, permanent joint-stock established — marks transition to modern corporate form

concepts.name: Joint-Stock Structure of EIC: Innovation and UPSC Misconceptions
key_dimensions: Early EIC (1600–1613): separate stock raised for each voyage — NOT true joint-stock; investors got returns per voyage
Transition to permanent joint-stock: only from 1657 under Cromwell's Charter — common trap: students assume it was always joint-stock
Significance: permanent stock enabled long-term planning, infrastructure, and eventually territorial ambitions
Comparison: VOC had permanent joint-stock from 1602 — Dutch structural advantage in early competition

concepts.name: EIC's Early Presidency System: Surat, Madras, and Bombay
key_dimensions: Surat (1613): first presidency/headquarters — western coast focus initially
Madras/Fort St. George (1639–1640): first fortified settlement — Francis Day negotiated with local Nayak ruler, NOT Mughal grant
Bombay (1661): received by English Crown as dowry from Portugal (marriage of Catherine of Braganza to Charles II), transferred to EIC in 1668 for £10/year — layered transaction UPSC loves
Calcutta/Fort William (1690–1696): founded by Job Charnock — the eastern presidency; sequence of Surat→Madras→Bombay→Calcutta is frequently tested

concepts.name: Foundation of Madras (1639): First Fortified English Settlement
key_dimensions: Negotiated by Francis Day with the Nayak of Chandragiri (Vijayanagara successor state) — NOT a Mughal grant, an important distinction
Fort St. George built 1640 — first English fort in India; 'Madras' name origin debated (possibly from Madrasan/Madrasapatnam, a local village)
Significance: represented shift from purely trading 'factory' to fortified territorial presence — a qualitative change in EIC's nature
Madras became the seat of the Madras Presidency — one of the three original presidencies

concepts.name: Acquisition of Bombay (1661–1668): Crown-to-Company Transfer
key_dimensions: Received by English Crown from Portugal as part of Catherine of Braganza's dowry for marriage to Charles II in 1661 — diplomatic/matrimonial origin
Crown transferred Bombay to EIC in 1668 at a nominal rent of £10 per annum — marks direct Crown-Company property transaction
Gerald Aungier (Governor 1669–1677): real developer of Bombay, encouraged merchants and built institutions — 'true founder of Bombay' distinction from those who focus on 1661
Bombay replaced Surat as western presidency HQ in 1687 — chronological sequence for UPSC

concepts.name: EIC's Relationship with the Mughal Empire (Early Phase, 1608–1680)
key_dimensions: Mughals viewed EIC as revenue-generating traders, NOT political threats — this perception explains concessions given
Farman system: trading privileges granted by imperial firman, revocable — EIC's legal standing was always subject to Mughal pleasure, not a right
Child's War (1686–1690) under Josiah Child: EIC attempted to coerce Aurangzeb militarily — disastrous failure; Company humiliated and had to beg forgiveness
Post-Child's War lesson: EIC returned to trade, not coercion, until Plassey (1757) — an arc UPSC tests as 'phases of EIC-Mughal relations'

concepts.name: Child's War (1686–1690): First Failed Attempt at Territorial Aggression
key_dimensions: Josiah Child (Chairman of EIC) pursued aggressive policy — blockaded Mughal ports, attacked Mughal ships
Aurangzeb's response: expelled EIC from Surat, Masulipatnam, and Bombay; imprisoned EIC factors
Outcome: EIC completely defeated; had to send abject apology to Aurangzeb and pay reparations
Significance: proved EIC could NOT militarily challenge Mughal power in this period — contrast with post-Mughal decline era; UPSC trap on 'who won Child's War'

concepts.name: Portuguese Presence and Conflict with EIC: The First Rivalry
key_dimensions: Portuguese Estado da India (est. 1505) predated EIC by nearly a century — 'Cartaz' system (pass system) controlled Indian Ocean trade
EIC challenge to Portuguese maritime dominance: Battle of Swally (1612) as the symbolic break
Portuguese held Goa, Diu, Daman, Bassein — EIC never dislodged Portuguese from these enclaves (they remained Portuguese until 1961)
Irony: England received Bombay from Portugal (1661) through diplomacy, not conquest — cooperation after competition

concepts.name: Old Company vs. New Company: The 1698 Rival Charter and Merger (1702–1709)
key_dimensions: Parliament chartered a rival 'New East India Company' in 1698 — political and financial context (William III needed funds, sold charter)
Two English East India Companies operating simultaneously (1698–1709) — a rare and confusing situation UPSC exploits
Merger into the 'United Company of Merchants of England Trading to the East Indies' in 1709 — the entity that became the dominant EIC of the 18th century
Significance: shows Company's monopoly was never absolute and was politically contingent; Parliament could create competition

concepts.name: Spice Trade vs. Textile Trade: Evolution of EIC's Commercial Focus
key_dimensions: Original objective (1600): pepper and spices from Southeast Asia — India was secondary
Shift to Indian textiles (cotton, silk) by mid-17th century: demand in English and European markets
Introduction of Indian calicoes into England caused domestic textile industry backlash — Calico Acts of 1690 and 1720 restricted Indian textile imports
Irony: EIC's commercial success created political enemies at home — shows interplay of trade, industry, and legislation

concepts.name: EIC and Parliament: From Private Charter to Public Accountability (Pre-Regulating Act Phase)
key_dimensions: 1600–1657: Company operated almost entirely outside parliamentary control — purely royal charter entity
Post-Restoration (1660s): Parliament increasingly interested in regulating trade; debates on monopoly vs. free trade
EIC's political lobbying and corruption of MPs — 'Company interest' in Parliament as a historical phenomenon
Foundation for later Parliamentary intervention: Regulating Act (1773) and Pitt's India Act (1784) are the culmination of this tension — knowing the early phase contextualises the later
